entity: South Carolina Chapter of Trout Unlimited
stance_basis: letter explicitly requests delay of licensing and states project will have significant negative impacts on water quality and aquatic community
summary: The South Carolina Chapter of Trout Unlimited submitted detailed technical comments opposing the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project, raising concerns about stream habitat destruction, siltation impacts on Howard Creek's trout fishery and spawning runs, degradation of Lake Jocassee's cold-water trout habitat, and inadequate flow augmentation mitigation. The organization argued that insufficient data existed to assess the project's full impacts and requested that licensing be deferred until ongoing studies were completed.
complaint_summary: The organization argues that siltation will severely impact Howard Creek's reproductive trout fishery and spawning run, that flow augmentation is not feasible mitigation due to temperature constraints and insufficient flow capacity, and requests that licensing be deferred until all ongoing studies are completed and sufficient data is available to assess the project's complex impacts.

statement.text:
Of major concern in evaluation of the Bad Creek Project is the impact of sediment on the Howard Creek drainage. In spite of major siltation from road construction, geological investigations, etc., a small reproductive fishery still exists in the stream although greatly reduced from its past state. The documented spawning run of large rainbow and brown trout into the lower portions of the stream makes these impacts all the more serious. The physical smothering of spawn by fine grained silt is well documented in the literature as well as the major decreases in primary production and benthic organisms from such siltation.
See Section 2.2.2.2 and 3.1.2.3.

Ongoing studies of reproductive and nursery success in lower Howard Creek are presently being performed by South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources. Sufficient time has not exapsed since last winter's spawning for the results to be conclusive. Since there is a reproductive rainbow trout fishery in Howard Creek, it can be safely assumed that spawning will be successful. The biological productivity of lower Howard is presently reduced due to sedimentation. Therefore, the nursery success this summer will be reduced proportionately. The increasing value and popularity of this new and unique resource makes it imperative that sufficient time for studies be allowed prior to a decision on licensing. In no other way can the values involved be realistically assessed.
An analysis of the Applicant's proposal to augment the flow of Howard Creek has been performed. The intent is to use water from Bad Creek Reservoir by means of a conduit-control valve system. Water of the same temperature as the stream will not be available in the Bad Creek Reservoir due to pumping back of Jocassee waters, and the temperature increasing factors discussed previously. This will necessitate increasing the temperature of Howard Creek in order to increase its flow. Since temperature is the critical condition for design of the discharge flow, the

result will be that whenever the temperature of Howard Creek is below of F. (the chosen temperature limit) higher temperature Bad Creek Reservoir water would be added either until the mixed condition equals 70° F. or the mixed flow equals natural e inditions. From temperature data published in 'Water Quality Investations for the Howard Creek Basin" (June 1975), it appears that the natural temperature of the basin rarely approaches this stress temperature. The biological benefit of increasing flow, but at the same time increasing temperature above natural conditions, would seem of little value. If the flow were augmented only to the highest temperature observed at this stream section, the amount of augmentation would be proportionately less. Further, the South Carolina water laws will not allow temperature increases in excess of 3° F. for trout waters. With these constraints it does not appear that meaningful thow augmentation would be feasible for summer periods nor can this be considered mitigation for negative impacts.
Flow argumentation is discussed in Sections 3.2.2.3, 4.2.3, and 9.2.
See revised Sections 2.2.2.2. and 3.2.2.3.
The use of flow augmentation to flush sediment is suggested in several places but recent sediment studies in the basin indicate that extremely high (flood) flows are necessary to effectively suspend and transport sediment. The scope of the proposed augmentation structures would not appear capable of delivering

sufficient flow rate. This realization is even more significant since the shility of the stream system to flush sediment will be greatly reduced. Therefore, the impact of construction sediment and the recovery time of the stream would seem to be grossly underestimated by the Applicant.
Summary
The Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project will have significant negative impacts on the water quality and aquatic community of both the Howard Creek Basin and Lake Jocassee. More serious are the substantial questions raised by partially completed studies and the changing environment of the lake system itself. Throughout our analysis of potential project impacts, sufficient definitive data has always been unavailable to draw final conclusions on potential impacts. Much of the data necessary is being developed through ongoing studies. If licensing is approved prior to the completion of these studies, meaningful assessments of impacts cannot be made or addressed in the final Environmental Impact Statement.
With the recent beginning of a load management study by the Applicant, the basic need for this peaking installation itself is in question. This two-year study will provide more concrete

load projections which have been used to justify the entire project. Until this study has been completed, the validity of future loads estimates are of questionable value.
In summary, the entire analysis of this Project has left doubts of sufficient data to truly assess the complex nature of the lake and stream system and assign values to the negative impacts. It is, therefore, requested that sufficient time be allowed for the development of all necessary factual information on the points stated above prior to a decision on licensing.
